newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges healing after Simpson verdicts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges healing after Simpson verdicts.

text.p: Reflecting on U.S. racial divisions brought to the surface by the O.J. Simpson trials, President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday that Americans should "spend more time listening to each other."
Clinton also urged the public to respect the verdicts in Simpson's criminal and civil trials since "that's the system we have in America" and "get onto other things."

It was the president's first public comment on the verdict of a predominantly white civil court jury that Simpson was responsible for the deaths of his former wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman. The jury ordered the former football star to pay a total of $33.5 million in damages to the families of the victims of the 1994 murders.
Simpson, who became a bit-part actor and television personality after his professional football career, was acquitted of criminal charges by a predominantly black criminal court jury in 1995.

Clinton, who commented on the case in response to a reporter's question at an unrelated White House meeting on campaign finance reform, said he was "troubled" by the racial polarisation it showed. Polls indicated that most white Americans believed Simpson committed the murders even though he has steadfastly maintained his innocence, while a majority of blacks believed he was the victim of a police frame-up.

"I think the only answer to that is for us to spend more time listening to each other and try to put ourselves in each other's shoes and understand why we see the world in different ways," Clinton said.
He added that while the race-freighted public reaction to the Simpson verdicts was disturbing there was reason for optimism about U.S. social harmony overall.

"We have succeeded so far in managing the world's most multi-ethnically diverse democracy better than a lot of countries that are smaller than ours with fewer differences. This is a work that's never done," Clinton said.
